title: Study of Compounds: Sulphuric Acid
tagline: The contact process, the three personalities of one acid — dilute, dehydrating and oxidising — and why it is called the king of acids.

overview.intro: Sulphuric acid is made in greater quantity than any other chemical, and the reason is that it behaves in three different ways depending on how it is used. Dilute it behaves as a strong acid, concentrated it dehydrates and oxidises. This chapter starts with the contact process because its three conditions make a complete exam question by themselves, then separates the three characters of the acid with the experiments that show each one — sugar charring for dehydration, copper dissolving for oxidation — and finishes with the uses that follow from them.

facts.label: Contact process
facts.value: Sulphur dioxide is oxidised to sulphur trioxide over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst, then absorbed in acid.

facts.label: Catalyst
facts.value: Vanadium(V) oxide, chosen because it is cheaper and poisons less easily than platinum.

facts.label: Absorption
facts.value: SO3 is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid to give oleum, which is then diluted carefully.

facts.label: Three characters
facts.value: Dilute acid behaves as an acid; concentrated acid dehydrates and oxidises.

learningOutcomes: Describe the contact process with the conditions chosen and the reason for each.
Write the equations of the three stages of sulphuric acid manufacture and explain why SO3 is not absorbed directly in water.
Give the reactions of dilute sulphuric acid with metals, bases, carbonates and salts.
Demonstrate the dehydrating and oxidising actions of concentrated sulphuric acid with named examples.
Explain the safe dilution of the acid and give its principal industrial uses.

learn.title: The contact process in three stages

blocks.text: The contact process begins with sulphur, which is burned in air to give sulphur dioxide. The key step is the catalytic oxidation of that dioxide to sulphur trioxide over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at around 450 °C and moderate pressure — conditions chosen because the reaction is reversible and only that combination gives a useful yield at an acceptable rate. The third stage is the clever one: sulphur trioxide is not absorbed directly in water, because the reaction is so violently exothermic that it forms a fine acid mist that is hard to condense. Instead it is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid to give oleum, and the oleum is then diluted with water to give more sulphuric acid. That two-step absorption recovers essentially all of the trioxide and is the detail that separates a full answer from a partial one.

items: Stage 1: S + O2 → SO2, burning sulphur in excess air.
Stage 2: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3 over V2O5 at about 450 °C, a reversible reaction favoured by moderate pressure.
Stage 3: SO3 + H2SO4 → H2S2O7 (oleum), then H2S2O7 + H2O → 2H2SO4.
Direct absorption of SO3 in water is avoided because it forms a mist that will not condense.

items.note: Vanadium(V) oxide works efficiently at 450 °C and is not poisoned by traces of arsenic compounds, unlike platinum.
The gain in yield above moderate pressure does not justify the cost and hazard of stronger vessels.

learn.title: Dilute sulphuric acid: the ordinary strong acid

blocks.text: Diluted to the strength of a normal acid, sulphuric acid behaves exactly as the definition requires, and it does so in two stages because it has two replaceable hydrogen atoms per molecule. With reactive metals above hydrogen it gives the metal sulphate and hydrogen; with metals such as copper it does nothing, because it lies below hydrogen. With bases it gives sulphate and water, with carbonates it gives sulphate, water and carbon dioxide, and with soluble barium salts it gives a white precipitate of barium sulphate — the reaction that identifies sulphate ions. Because the second replaceable hydrogen is lost less readily than the first, acid salts such as sodium hydrogen sulphate exist and are stable enough to isolate.

items: Metal + acid → metal sulphate + hydrogen, provided the metal is above hydrogen in the activity series.
Base + acid → sulphate + water, the standard neutralisation.
Carbonate + acid → sulphate + water + carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky.
Barium chloride or barium nitrate gives white barium sulphate insoluble in dilute acid, the confirmatory test for sulphate.

items.note: Zn + H2SO4 → ZnSO4 + H2, with hydrogen confirmed by the squeaky pop.
BaCl2 + H2SO4 → BaSO4 + 2HCl; the white precipitate does not dissolve when dilute acid is added.

learn.title: The dehydrating agent: sugar, paper and blue vitriol

blocks.text: Concentrated sulphuric acid has such an affinity for water that it will remove the elements of water from compounds that are not wet at all. The demonstration that everyone remembers is sugar: pour the acid onto white sugar and a black column of carbon rises out of the beaker, because the acid has stripped hydrogen and oxygen in the ratio two to one from sucrose and left the carbon behind. The same action chars paper and wood, and it converts blue copper sulphate crystals to a white anhydrous powder — which is also the standard test for water. The acid must be handled with care in these demonstrations because the reaction is strongly exothermic and the acid is corrosive, but the chemistry is the same every time: water is removed from a compound, not from a mixture.

items: Sugar turns to black carbon: C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O, the water being taken up by the acid.
Blue copper sulphate crystals turn white as the water of crystallisation is removed.
Cellulose in paper and wood is dehydrated, leaving carbon, which is why the residue is black.
The reaction is exothermic; steam and heat are given off and the mixture swells as gases escape.

items.note: Sugar swells into a black spongy mass, with heat and steam released as the acid dehydrates it.
A few drops on white paper that leaves a brown mark suggest water or another hydroxyl-rich liquid has been removed.

items.meaning: Removal of hydrogen and oxygen as water from a compound by a strong dehydrating agent.
Strong tendency of concentrated sulphuric acid to combine with water, driving reactions to completion.
Water-free, as in white copper sulphate after its water of crystallisation is removed.

learn.title: Oxidising action, dilution safety and storage

blocks.text: The concentrated acid is also a powerful oxidiser: when it attacks a metal it does not release hydrogen but oxidises it to water while the sulphate itself is reduced, usually to sulphur dioxide. Copper dissolves with the liberation of choking sulphur dioxide and gives a blue solution of copper(II) sulphate; carbon is oxidised to carbon dioxide; sulphur to sulphuric acid itself. This oxidising power is why the acid attacks metals that dilute acid cannot touch. The same character dictates the safety rules. Concentrated sulphuric acid must never be poured into water without care — it must be added slowly to water with stirring, never the reverse, because the enormous heat released when it hydrates would boil the water and spatter concentrated acid. The acid is stored in glass or in lined steel, and because it is non-volatile it can be kept in open vessels in the laboratory.

items: Copper + concentrated acid gives copper sulphate, sulphur dioxide and water, not hydrogen.
Carbon oxidises to carbon dioxide and sulphur to sulphuric acid under the same conditions.
Dilution: add the acid slowly to water with constant stirring; never add water to concentrated acid.
The hydration releases so much heat that water added to the acid boils and throws the acid out of the vessel.

items.note: The metal dissolves, brown fumes of sulphur dioxide appear and a blue solution remains.
Acid poured slowly into a beaker of water with stirring stays cool enough to handle safely.

items.meaning: Acid that accepts electrons from the substance it attacks, as concentrated sulphuric acid does.
Choking gas SO2 produced when concentrated sulphuric acid is reduced by a metal or non-metal.
Large amount of heat released when concentrated acid combines with water, the reason dilution must be controlled.

learn.title: Uses of sulphuric acid and why the question always returns

blocks.text: Roughly half of all sulphuric acid is used to make fertilisers, where it converts phosphate rock into a soluble phosphate that plants can absorb. The rest spreads across petroleum refining to remove impurities, metallurgy where it leaches metals from ores, the manufacture of hydrochloric and nitric acids where it acts as the less volatile acid, and car batteries where dilute acid stores the charge. Its dehydrating ability makes it a drying agent for gases, and its oxidising ability supports dye and explosive manufacture. Examiners ask for uses because they are the economic justification for the contact process itself: a question about the process and a question about uses are really the same question from two angles, so learn three uses each tied to one of the acid’s three characters.

items: Fertilisers: conversion of insoluble phosphate rock into soluble superphosphate.
Other acids: it displaces the more volatile hydrochloric and nitric acids from their salts.
Petroleum refining and metal extraction: removal of impurities and leaching of ores.
Storage batteries and laboratory drying: dilute acid for the battery, concentrated acid for drying gases.

items.note: Rock phosphate treated with sulphuric acid yields a soluble phosphate fertilizer crop roots can take up.

items.text: Drying agent in a gas train
items.note: Concentrated acid in a wash bottle dries hydrogen or carbon dioxide before collection.

blocks.caption: Property behind each use
rows: Less volatile than HCl and HNO3
Displaces them from their salts in the laboratory

keyPoints: The contact process: burn sulphur to SO2, oxidise it over V2O5 near 450 °C, absorb the SO3 in concentrated acid.
SO3 is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid rather than water because direct absorption forms an uncondensable mist.
Dilute sulphuric acid gives metal sulphate and hydrogen with reactive metals, salt and water with bases, and salt, water and carbon dioxide with carbonates.
Barium chloride gives white barium sulphate insoluble in dilute acid: the confirmatory test for sulphate.
Concentrated sulphuric acid dehydrates sugar, wood and hydrated crystals, leaving carbon or anhydrous salts.
Concentrated sulphuric acid oxidises copper, carbon and sulphur, being reduced itself to sulphur dioxide.
Dilution is always acid into water with stirring, because hydration releases intense heat.
The acid is non-volatile and can be stored in open glass vessels in the laboratory.
Major uses: fertiliser manufacture, other acids, refining, leaching, batteries and drying.
Acid salts such as sodium hydrogen sulphate exist because the two replaceable hydrogens are lost in stages.
examFocus: The contact process is three numbered stages; give reagents, conditions and one reason for each choice.
Explain why SO3 goes into acid and not water — the mist argument is a standard two-mark answer.
The sugar experiment is asked as an observation plus deduction: black carbon proves dehydration, not burning.
Safety answers must state the direction of mixing explicitly: acid added slowly to water, never the reverse.

vocabulary.meaning: Industrial route to sulphuric acid via catalytic oxidation of sulphur dioxide.
Substance that speeds a reaction without being consumed, here vanadium(V) oxide.
Solution of sulphur trioxide in concentrated sulphuric acid, fuming sulphuric acid.
Substance that removes hydrogen and oxygen as water from compounds.
Substance that accepts electrons, here the concentrated acid reduced to sulphur dioxide.
SO4 2-, identified by a white barium sulphate precipitate insoluble in acid.
Releasing heat, as hydration of concentrated sulphuric acid strongly does.
Acid cleaning of metal surfaces, one of the acid’s industrial uses.

questions.prompt: The catalyst used in the contact process is:
questions.explanation: Vanadium(V) oxide is active at about 450 °C and resists poisoning by impurities better than platinum.

questions.prompt: Sulphur trioxide is absorbed in concentrated sulphuric acid rather than in water because:
options: Direct absorption forms a fine acid mist that will not condense
The acid is cheaper than water
questions.answer: Direct absorption forms a fine acid mist that will not condense
questions.explanation: The hydration is violently exothermic and produces a suspended droplet mist, so oleum formation avoids it.

questions.prompt: Concentrated sulphuric acid added to sugar makes the sugar:
options: Turn black as carbon is left behind
questions.answer: Turn black as carbon is left behind
questions.explanation: The acid removes hydrogen and oxygen as water from sucrose, leaving elemental carbon as a black mass.

questions.prompt: When copper is heated with concentrated sulphuric acid the gases given off is:
questions.explanation: The concentrated acid oxidises the metal and is itself reduced to sulphur dioxide, not to hydrogen.

questions.prompt: When diluting concentrated sulphuric acid, the acid must be added slowly to __________ with stirring.
questions.explanation: Adding water to the dense acid would boil the water on contact and throw acid out of the vessel.

questions.prompt: The solution of sulphuric trioxide in concentrated sulphuric acid is known as __________.
questions.explanation: Oleum is diluted carefully with water to give more sulphuric acid without forming a mist.

questions.prompt: Give the equation for the catalytic oxidation stage of the contact process and the conditions used.
questions.answer: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3, carried out over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at about 450 °C and moderate pressure; the reaction is reversible so the conditions are a compromise between rate and yield.
questions.explanation: The forward reaction is exothermic and favoured by lower temperature, but the rate requires the higher chosen value.

questions.prompt: Describe a test that confirms the sulphate ion in solution.
questions.answer: Add barium chloride solution to the acidified solution: a white precipitate of barium sulphate forms and it does not dissolve in dilute hydrochloric acid, which distinguishes sulphate from carbonate or sulphite.
questions.explanation: Barium sulphate is insoluble in acid while the other barium salts dissolve with effervescence or gas evolution.

questions.prompt: Name one property of concentrated sulphuric acid that explains its use as a drying agent for gases.
questions.answer: It has a very strong affinity for water and combines with it eagerly, so it removes water vapour from hydrogen, carbon dioxide and similar gases passed over it.
questions.explanation: A drying agent must bind water more strongly than the gas being dried does.

questions.prompt: Describe the contact process for sulphuric acid, giving each stage with its conditions and explaining the final absorption step.
questions.answer: Sulphur is burned in excess air to give sulphur dioxide. The gas is purified, mixed with more air and passed over a vanadium(V) oxide catalyst at about 450 °C under moderate pressure, where it oxidises reversibly to sulphur trioxide: 2SO2 + O2 ⇌ 2SO3. Rather than absorbing the trioxide in water, which would produce a fog of droplets that cannot be condensed, it is dissolved in concentrated sulphuric acid to form oleum, H2S2O7. The oleum is then diluted with water to give concentrated sulphuric acid of the required strength, and any unconverted sulphur dioxide is recycled to the converter.
questions.explanation: Three stages with reasons: catalysis for rate, compromise conditions for yield, and oleum absorption to avoid mist and maximise recovery.

questions.prompt: Explain, with an equation, what happens when concentrated sulphuric acid is poured onto cane sugar, and state what the observation proves.
questions.answer: The acid dehydrates the sucrose: C12H22O11 → 12C + 11H2O, with the liberated water taken up by the acid and a great deal of heat released. The white sugar swells into a black spongy mass of carbon, steam and acid fumes escaping as the reaction runs up the beaker. The observation proves that concentrated sulphuric acid removes the elements of water from a compound without burning it: no flame is present and no oxygen is supplied from outside, so the carbon left behind must have come from the decomposition of the sugar itself.
questions.explanation: Formation of carbon without combustion shows chemical dehydration rather than oxidation by air.

questions.prompt: A colourless acid gives a white precipitate with barium chloride that is insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid, and with copper it produces a choking gas when heated. Identify the acid, the precipitate and the gas, and explain why copper does not react with the dilute acid.
questions.answer: The sulphate test identifies sulphuric acid, and the white precipitate is barium sulphate, which is insoluble in acid because its lattice energy makes it exceptionally stable. Heating copper with the concentrated acid gives sulphur dioxide, the choking gas, because the concentrated acid oxidises copper while being reduced itself. With dilute acid no reaction occurs: copper lies below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from a dilute acid, whereas the concentrated acid attacks it by an oxidation mechanism that does not depend on displacing hydrogen.
questions.explanation: Two independent signs identify the acid and its concentrated character, and the copper difference rests on activity series versus oxidising power.
